young.html: The Phaedo tells the story of Socrates' last day. His friends came to the prison early in the morning, because they knew it was the day the sentence would be carried out. Some of them were crying. Socrates was calm, and even cheerful.

He spent the day doing what he loved most: talking and asking questions. The big question was this: does the soul go on living after the body dies? Socrates believed it does, and he tried to give reasons, not just say so. His friends Simmias and Cebes raised objections, and he welcomed them.

One of his arguments used opposites. Sleeping turns into waking, and waking into sleeping. Small things grow large, and large things can shrink. Things come from their opposites. So, Socrates asked, if living things die, might the dead also come back to life?

young.name: gb-opposites
young.cap: Pick a pair of opposites. Each one turns into the other by its own road.

young.html: Opposites hunt. List as many pairs of opposites as you can in five minutes (hot and cold, full and empty, wet and dry…). For each pair, name the change that goes each way: what turns hot into cold? What turns cold into hot? Are there any pairs where the change only goes one way?
Socrates said that swans sing most beautifully just before they die, not out of sadness but out of joy. People still call someone's last great work a “swan song.”

full.html: Plato's Phaedo (written about 380s BC) is told by Phaedo, one of the young men who were there, to a friend named Echecrates some time afterward. Phaedo lists who came. Plato himself was absent: “Plato, if I am not mistaken, was ill,” Phaedo says (in Jowett’s translation), a small and moving touch from the author.

Socrates' wife Xanthippe is there at dawn with their youngest child, and Socrates has her taken home. He tells his friends that he has been setting Aesop's fables to verse, because a dream kept telling him to “make music.” Then the conversation turns serious.

Why is Socrates not afraid? He says a lover of wisdom spends his life trying to see things with the mind, not the body's senses, and death, as he believes, is the soul's release from the body. So a philosopher has been rehearsing all along:

full.text: And the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying, wherefore also to them least of all men is death terrible.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

head: Argument
In brief
The objection it faces
rows: Everything that has an opposite comes from that opposite, so the living come from the dead, as the dead from the living.
It shows at most that souls return; Cebes wants to know that they last.
We recognize two sticks as “equal” but not perfectly equal, so we must already know Equality itself. We learned it before birth.
This shows the soul existed before birth, not that it survives death.
The soul is like the unseen, unchanging and divine; the body is like the seen and changing. So the soul is not the kind of thing that scatters.
Simmias: maybe the soul is like the tuning of a lyre, which vanishes when the lyre breaks.
The soul brings life to whatever it is in, as fire brings heat. So it cannot admit death, as fire cannot admit cold.
Socrates himself says the starting points need further study.
full.cap: The arguments of the Phaedo, in our own words.

full.text: Are not all things which have opposites generated out of their opposites? I mean such things as good and evil, just and unjust—and there are innumerable other opposites which are generated out of opposites.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press
full.note: The margin notes of the printed edition are left out.

full.name: gb-opposites
full.cap: The first argument: each pair of opposites is joined by two roads. Socrates asks what would happen if the change ran only one way.

full.html: Simmias and Cebes go quiet, worried that their doubts will upset him on such a day. Socrates laughs and says he is no more troubled than a swan:

full.text: Will you not allow that I have as much of the spirit of prophecy in me as the swans? For they, when they perceive that they must die, having sung all their life long, do then sing more lustily than ever, rejoicing in the thought that they are about to go away to the god whose ministers they are.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: Simmias says the soul might be a kind of harmony, like the tuning of a lyre. Cebes says it might be like a weaver who wears out many cloaks and then dies: it outlasts many bodies but not for ever. At this low point Socrates warns against becoming a “hater of arguments” (a misologist) just because some arguments fail. The fault, he says, is in our skill, not in reasoning itself.

Before his last argument, Socrates tells how, as a young man, he hoped the philosopher Anaxagoras would explain why things are as they are, by showing what is best. He was disappointed: Anaxagoras explained only the bones and muscles, so to speak, not the reasons. So Socrates turned to a “second voyage”: looking for causes in the Forms, such as Beauty itself and Largeness itself.

Thinking the Phaedo proves the soul is immortal. Socrates offers arguments and says they deserve more testing; he ends with a story about the next world and says only that a sensible man would not insist it is exactly true, but that it is worth the risk of believing something like it.

At sunset Socrates bathes, says goodbye to his family, and drinks the cup when the jailer brings it, as the law requires. He asks Crito to offer a rooster to Asclepius, the god of healing; readers still debate what he meant. Phaedo ends:

full.text: Such was the end, Echecrates, of our friend; concerning whom I may truly say, that of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

deep.html: The Phaedo is one of the first dialogues to rely on what are now called Plato's Forms: Equality itself, Beauty itself, Justice itself, perfect and unchanging, which particular things only resemble. The recollection argument here links back to the Meno, where a boy “recollects” geometry. The Republic, later on this ladder, builds the Forms into a whole picture of knowledge.

Aristotle, in On the Soul, describes the soul as the form of a living body, which made the question of its surviving the body much harder. Plotinus and Augustine, later on this ladder, drew on the Phaedo, each in his own way. Some modern readers find the arguments weak but the portrait of Socrates' calm unforgettable; others think the arguments are better than they first look. The harmony objection anticipates the modern view that the mind depends on the brain, and the dialogue is still read in courses on that question.

items: Is it possible to face death without fear? What helped Socrates?
If an argument for something you hope is true turns out weak, should you stop believing it, keep looking for better arguments, or both?
Socrates warned against “hating arguments.” Have you ever given up on reasoning because one argument let you down?

questions: Socrates' friends were sad, but he was calm. Why do you think he felt that way?
What other opposites can you think of? Do they really turn into each other?
Simmias compared the soul to the music of a lyre. Is that a good comparison? Why or why not?
What is a “swan song”? Can you think of an example?
Phaedo calls Socrates “the wisest and justest and best.” What would you like people to say about you?
care: This dialogue is about death, and it ends with Socrates drinking poison, as his sentence required. Plato tells it gently, without anything graphic. It presents Socrates' own beliefs about the soul; families will want to talk about their own.
